documents.title: ATA Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and DTC

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Pediatric thyroid cancer is relatively rarer than its adult counterpart. According to data from the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) registry, the age-standardized incidence rates of thyroid cancer in children are 1.14 per 100,000 person-years in the United States [ ] and 0.92 per 100,000 person-years in Korea [ ]. By contrast, the incidence of adult thyroid cancer is 14.6 per 100,000 person-years according to the SEER database, representing an incidence approximately 13–15 times higher than that observed in children [ ]. While a recent increase in incidence has been reported, with an annual percent change of 4.0%–9.5% from the 2000s to the mid-2010s, a similar trend has also been observed in the adult population [ ]. Despite its rarity, pediatric thyroid cancer exhibits distinct clinical and molecular characteristics that allow differentiation from adult thyroid cancer [ ]. In children, the likelihood of malignancy when a thyroid nodule is present is notably higher than in adults, ranging from 22%–26% compared with 5%–10% in adults [ ]. With respect to molecular profiles, BRAF V600E mutations, which are commonly observed in adult thyroid cancer (49%–62%) [ ], are less frequently reported in pediatric thyroid cancer (20%–39%) [ ]. Instead, gene fusions involving RET or NTRK are more prevalent, particularly in younger children [ ]. In addition, pediatric patients are more likely to present with advanced disease at diagnosis. Regional lymph node metastases occur in approximately 60%–80% of pediatric thyroid cancers, compared with 20%–50% of thyroid cancers in adults, and distant metastases are reported in 5%–25% of pediatric patients, in comparison with typical rates of 2%–5% in adults [ ]. Another important consideration is the smaller thyroid gland volume in children; therefore, a tumor of the same absolute size may occupy a greater proportion of the thyroid in pediatric patients [ ], potentially increasing the likelihood of capsular invasion or extension into adjacent vital structures. However, despite a typically more aggressive initial presentation, the prognosis of pediatric thyroid cancer is generally more favorable than that of thyroid cancer in adults [ ]. All-stage mortality is less than 1% in children, compared with 1%–2% in adults [ ]. Moreover, in the setting of distant metastasis, mortality rates in children remain between 1%–7%, which is substantially lower than the rates of at least 20% observed in adults [ ]. This improved prognosis may be attributable to several factors, including the predominance of well-differentiated tumor histology, a lower incidence of bone metastases, and a favorable response to radioactive iodine therapy in the pediatric population. Given these biological and clinical differences, it may not be appropriate to apply adult-based management guidelines to pediatric thyroid cancer. In this context, the Korean Society of Thyroid Radiology published the 2021 Korean Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (K-TIRADS), which reflects the unique characteristics of the pediatric population. Accordingly, this review aims to present the background and details of the 2021 K-TIRADS from a pediatric-specific perspective, highlight the need for tailored diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, and discuss future refinements of pediatric-specific ultrasound (US) risk-stratification systems. APPLICATION OF ADULT-BASED ULTRASOUND RISK-STRATIFICATION SYSTEMS IN CHILDREN BEFORE THE 2021 K-TIRADS The primary consideration for radiologists when evaluating thyroid nodules is estimating the likelihood of malignancy and determining the necessity for biopsy. Several international societies have proposed US-based stratification systems that utilize sonographic features, including composition, echogenicity, shape, orientation, margins, and echogenic foci, to classify nodules according to their malignancy risk. Based on the assigned category, different size thresholds were proposed to guide decisions regarding the requirements for fine-needle aspiration biopsy, making this stratification a cornerstone of nodule management. Commonly used US risk-stratification systems include the American College of Radiology TIRADS (ACR TI-RADS) [ ], American Association of Clinical Endocrinology/American College of Endocrinology/Associazione Medici Endocrinologi (AACE/ACE/AME) Medical Guidelines for Clinical Practice for the Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Nodules-2016 Update [ ], American Thyroid Association (ATA) Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer [ ], European TIRADS (EU-TIRADS) [ ], and Chinese TIRADS (C-TIRADS) [ ]. Although several guidelines include pediatric-specific descriptions, these systems were mainly developed using adult populations, raising concerns about their direct application to children ( ). In 2021, a meta-analysis evaluated studies that investigated the diagnostic accuracy of the ACR TIRADS and ATA guidelines when directly applied to children [ ]. When category 4 or 5 was defined as a positive index test for the ACR TI-RADS, the pooled sensitivity was 84% (95% CI: 78%–89%) and the pooled specificity was 64% (95% CI: 41%–81%). For the ATA system, considering high- or intermediate-suspicion nodules as a positive index test yielded a pooled sensitivity of 90% (95% CI: 83%–94%) and a specificity of 50% (95% CI: 32%–68%). For ACR-TIRADS, the pooled missed malignancy and unnecessary biopsy rates were 21.7% and 62.7%, respectively, which are relatively high

the diagnostic accuracy of the ACR TIRADS and ATA guidelines when directly applied to children [ ]. When category 4 or 5 was defined as a positive index test for the ACR TI-RADS, the pooled sensitivity was 84% (95% CI: 78%–89%) and the pooled specificity was 64% (95% CI: 41%–81%). For the ATA system, considering high- or intermediate-suspicion nodules as a positive index test yielded a pooled sensitivity of 90% (95% CI: 83%–94%) and a specificity of 50% (95% CI: 32%–68%). For ACR-TIRADS, the pooled missed malignancy and unnecessary biopsy rates were 21.7% and 62.7%, respectively, which are relatively high values, indicating that the direct application of adult-based risk stratification systems is questionable. Kim et al. [ ] evaluated 277 nodules from 221 pediatric patients who underwent percutaneous biopsy and compared the diagnostic performances of the ACR TI-RADS, AACE/ACE/AME, ATA, EU-TIRADS, and 2016 K-TIRADS. In detail, the sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were as follows: ACR TI-RADS: 70% (95% CI: 62%–77%), 78% (95% CI: 70%–84%), and 74% (95% CI: 68%–78%), respectively; ATA: 77% (95% CI: 69%–83%), 42% (95% CI: 34%–51%), and 61% (95% CI: 55%–67%); AACE/ACE/AME: 76% (95% CI: 68%–83%), 51% (95% CI: 42%–59%), and 65% (95% CI: 59%–70%); EU-TIRADS: 76% (95% CI: 68%–83%), 46% (95% CI: 37%–54%), and 62% (95% CI: 56%–68%); 2016 K-TIRADS: 78% (95% CI: 71%–84%), 43% (95% CI: 35%–52%), and 62% (95% CI: 57%–68%). Using the biopsy recommendation as a positive index test, ACR TI-RADS demonstrated the highest overall diagnostic accuracy (74% vs. 61%–65%) and specificity among the evaluated systems (78% vs. 42%–51%). Similarly, in other studies, the ACR TI-RADS showed higher specificity than the ATA guideline [ ] or EU-TIRADS [ ], except for the study by Tuli et al. [ ], in which the EU-TIRADS showed slightly higher specificity than the ACR TI-RADS (57% vs. 50%). This higher specificity was likely due to the relatively higher biopsy cutoff sizes applied to moderately and mildly suspicious nodules in the ACR TI-RADS, given that biopsy cutoff sizes are a well-established factor influencing diagnostic accuracy in risk-stratification systems [ ]. In all five risk-stratification systems, the biopsy cutoff size for the highest category was 1 cm. However, the biopsy cut-off sizes differ in the next highest category: ACR TI-RADS recommends biopsy for moderately suspicious nodules ≥1.5 cm, whereas the ATA and 2016 K-TIRADS recommend biopsy for intermediate-suspicion nodules ≥1 cm. In addition, ACR TI-RADS recommends biopsy for mildly suspicious nodules ≥2.5 cm, while the ATA guideline and 2016 K-TIRADS recommend biopsy for low-suspicion nodules ≥1.5 cm, and EU-TIRADS recommends biopsy for low-risk nodules ≥2 cm. This indicates that, even in pediatric thyroid nodules, increasing the biopsy size cutoff for categories with a low risk of cancer may help reduce unnecessary biopsy rates, thereby leading to a higher overall accuracy. In contrast, the risk of malignancy in the highest category was higher in pediatric patients. Kim et al. [ ] reported that the risk of malignancy in the highest category of pediatric thyroid nodules ranged from 85.4% to 94.0% (93.2% for ACR TI-RADS, 93.4% for ATA, 85.4% for AACE/ACE/AME, 86.0% for EU TIRADS, and 94.0% for 2016 K TIRADS). Considering that the corresponding risk in adults ranges from 32.3% to 66.1% [ ], the values in the pediatric population were high. This suggests that lowering the biopsy size cutoff for the highest category could enhance sensitivity and minimize missed malignancies without substantial tradeoffs in specificity or unnecessary biopsy rates. These findings suggest that a two-track approach, that is, lowering the biopsy cutoff size for the highest-category nodules while raising the biopsy cutoff size for nodules in relatively lower categories, could be effective in pediatric patients. Kim et al. [ ] demonstrated that when all nodules in the highest category were biopsied (regardless of nodule size) rather than just those over the conventional 1-cm threshold, the sensitivity increased by 13%–18%. In addition, when the ACR TI-RADS biopsy criteria were applied to the other guidelines, the specificity improved by 7%–37%. Notably, the overall accuracy was the highest when both strategies were combined, with a 5%–20% improvement compared with the original versions. APPLICATION OF THE 2021 K-TIRADS TO CHILDREN When adult-based US risk stratification systems have been applied to pediatric populations, they have shown suboptimal diagnostic accuracy, suggesting that further modifications are necessary. These modifications can include adjustments of biopsy size cutoff thresholds, incorporation of clinical risk factors, such as a family history of cancer or prior irradiation, and integration of specific US characteristics of the diffuse sclerosing subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma, which is more prevalent in pediatric papillary thyroid cancers (PTCs) [ ]. In this context, the Korean Society of Thyroid Radiology released an updated 2021 version of the K-TIRADS, which revised the guidelines established in 2016 [ ]. The major changes in K-TIRADS from 2016 to 2021 are summarized

have shown suboptimal diagnostic accuracy, suggesting that further modifications are necessary. These modifications can include adjustments of biopsy size cutoff thresholds, incorporation of clinical risk factors, such as a family history of cancer or prior irradiation, and integration of specific US characteristics of the diffuse sclerosing subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma, which is more prevalent in pediatric papillary thyroid cancers (PTCs) [ ]. In this context, the Korean Society of Thyroid Radiology released an updated 2021 version of the K-TIRADS, which revised the guidelines established in 2016 [ ]. The major changes in K-TIRADS from 2016 to 2021 are summarized in . The 2021 K-TIRADS introduced several refinements to the US lexicon to improve diagnostic consistency, interobserver agreement, and clinical applicability. In the 2016 K-TIRADS, marked hypoechogenicity was defined as echogenicity lower than that of the anterior neck muscles; in the 2021 K-TIRADS, this category was expanded to include nodules with similar echogenicity relative to the anterior neck muscles, based on evidence demonstrating comparable malignancy risk between these nodules [ ] and the practical difficulty in reliably distinguishing these echogenicity levels [ ]. In the 2016 K-TIRADS, mild hypoechogenicity was defined as hypoechoic relative to the surrounding thyroid parenchyma, whereas in the 2021 K-TIRADS, normal thyroid parenchyma was used as the reference to avoid misclassification in cases of diffuse thyroid disease. Notably, the terminology for calcifications was revised to echogenic foci, acknowledging that echogenic foci may represent inspissated colloids as well as microcalcifications. Additionally, orientation assessment was standardized to the transverse plane, as prior evidence demonstrated no significant difference in the diagnostic accuracy of the K-TIRADS biopsy criteria according to the imaging plane used [ ]. Finally, margin descriptors were simplified by integrating spiculated or microlobulated margins into the category of irregular margins, thereby enhancing the reporting clarity and consistency. The 2021 K-TIRADS also revised the biopsy size cutoff criteria for pediatric patients. The biopsy size cut-off for high-suspicion nodules in children was reduced from 1.0 cm to 0.5 cm, whereas the cut-off for intermediate-suspicion nodules was increased from 1.0 cm to 1.5 cm (in the absence of specific risk factors), and that for low-suspicion nodules was increased from 1.5 cm to 2.0 cm. In addition, when the patient has certain risk factors, such as [ 18 F]fluorodeoxyglucose avidity on PET scan, familial cancer (e.g., DICER1 syndrome, MEN type 2, Cowden syndrome), worrisome symptoms (e.g., dysphonia), worrisome nodule locations (e.g., attachment to the trachea or the posteromedial capsule along the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve), or patient-specific factors (e.g., age, comorbidities, and personal preference), the biopsy size cut-off for intermediate-suspicion nodules can be lowered to 1.0 cm. In children, the 2021 K-TIRADS demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity (90.3% vs. 81.2%; P = 0.004), specificity (47.9% vs. 37.0%; P < 0.001), and accuracy (68.9% vs. 58.4%; P = 0.01) than the 2016 K-TIRADS ( ) [ ]. When the biopsy cut-off sizes for other categories were held constant, the application of a 0.5-cm biopsy cut-off size for high-suspicion nodules in the 2021 version resulted in slightly lower specificity (47.9% vs. 51.6%; P = 0.004) but higher sensitivity (90.3% vs. 77.2%; P < 0.001) and accuracy (68.9% vs. 62.7%; P < 0.001) compared to using a 1.0-cm biopsy cut-off size. Similarly, when a 1.0–1.5-cm biopsy cutoff size was applied to intermediate-suspicion nodules while the biopsy cutoff sizes for other categories were held constant, there was no significant difference in sensitivity (90.3% vs. 91.6%; P = 0.063) or accuracy (68.9% vs. 68.0%; P = 0.436); however, the specificity was slightly higher (47.9% vs. 44.9%; P = 0.018), as described in [ ]. This supports the effectiveness of the two-track approach advocated by the 2021 K-TIRADS, which lowers the biopsy cutoff size for high-suspicion nodules while increasing it for intermediate- to low-suspicion nodules. OTHER ATTEMPTS TO MODIFY EXISTING ULTRASOUND RISK-STRATIFICATION SYSTEMS FOR PEDIATRIC APPLICATIONS Similar to the recent revisions in the K-TIRADS, several other efforts have been made to improve the diagnostic performance of US risk-stratification systems in pediatric populations. Among these, the ACR TI-RADS is the most extensively studied system. summarizes the diagnostic performance of the original ACR TI-RADS and various studies that evaluated modified biopsy cutoff size strategies [ ]. These modifications include lowering the biopsy threshold for TR5 nodules to 0.5 cm or performing a biopsy for any TR5 nodule when technically feasible, as well as lowering or conversely increasing the biopsy cutoff for TR3 or TR4 nodules. Srivatsa et al. [ ] modified the ACR TI-RADS biopsy thresholds as follows: TR5: from 1.0 cm to any size if technically feasible; TR4: from 1.5 cm to 1.0 cm; TR3: from 2.5 cm to 1.5 cm. These modifications resulted in an increase in sensitivity from 94.6% to 100%, a decrease in specificity from 71.9% to 55.3%, and a decrease in the overall

include lowering the biopsy threshold for TR5 nodules to 0.5 cm or performing a biopsy for any TR5 nodule when technically feasible, as well as lowering or conversely increasing the biopsy cutoff for TR3 or TR4 nodules. Srivatsa et al. [ ] modified the ACR TI-RADS biopsy thresholds as follows: TR5: from 1.0 cm to any size if technically feasible; TR4: from 1.5 cm to 1.0 cm; TR3: from 2.5 cm to 1.5 cm. These modifications resulted in an increase in sensitivity from 94.6% to 100%, a decrease in specificity from 71.9% to 55.3%, and a decrease in the overall accuracy from 75.4% to 62.3%. Similarly, Marzukie et al. [ ] reduced the biopsy cutoff sizes for TR3, TR4, and TR5 nodules, leading to an increase in sensitivity from 83.3% to 94.4%, a decrease in specificity from 75.5% to 63.3%, and a decrease in accuracy from 76.7% to 68.1%. Although an increase in sensitivity would promote the early detection of pediatric thyroid cancer and reduce the likelihood of missed malignancy, it comes at the cost of increasing unnecessary biopsy rates. Furthermore, considering that pediatric thyroid cancer tends to present with higher rates of regional lymph node and distant metastases at diagnosis yet does not generally confer poorer survival, it remains unclear whether such an increase in sensitivity is truly beneficial. Thus, further studies focusing on clinically meaningful outcomes, such as patient prognosis, are warranted. Another approach is to lower the biopsy cutoff size in pediatric patients with known risk factors for thyroid cancer. Although this strategy is partly incorporated into the 2021 K-TIRADS, which recommends reducing the biopsy threshold for K-TIRADS 4 nodules from 1.5 cm to 1.0 cm in patients at risk of thyroid cancer, data supporting similar approaches in other US risk-stratification systems are still limited. In a simulation study by Lee et al. [ ], the biopsy cut-off sizes for K-TIRADS and ACR TI-RADS category 4 nodules were further reduced to 0.5 cm in patients with risk factors. In the study, the authors found that the specificity of the K-TIRADS decreased slightly from 59% to 53%; however, the sensitivity increased from 78% to 85%, leading to an improvement in accuracy (71% to 74%). Similarly, when the biopsy threshold for ACR TI-RADS category 4 nodules with risk factors was lowered from 1.5 cm to 0.5 cm, specificity decreased from 80% to 65%, while sensitivity increased from 60% to 84%. This change resulted in an overall accuracy improvement from 67% to 77% ( ). Therefore, risk factor-adapted modifications may be a viable option for future refinements of other US risk stratification systems. CONSIDERATIONS FOR FUTURE REFINEMENTS OF PEDIATRIC-SPECIFIC ULTRASOUND RISK-STRATIFICATION SYSTEMS Overdiagnosis: Pediatric-Specific Clinical Considerations Overdiagnosis is one of the most critical concerns in thyroid cancer. Although the incidence of thyroid cancer has steadily increased over the past two decades, the survival rates have remained largely unchanged [ ]. This trend suggests that the widespread use of ultrasonography has contributed to overdiagnosis and escalating medical costs. However, the actual clinical impact on patient outcomes remains questionable. Pediatric thyroid cancer exhibits paradoxical clinical characteristics [ ]. They are usually detected as large, rapidly growing tumors, often accompanied by lymph node and distant metastases, and show higher postoperative recurrence rates than thyroid cancers in adults. Nevertheless, the long-term prognosis in children remains excellent, with a lifespan survival rate exceeding 95%. Indeed, although the Fukushima Health Management Survey, which screened approximately 380,000 children after the nuclear accident, revealed an unexpectedly high prevalence of pediatric thyroid cancer (30/100,000) [ ], most of these cancers remained small throughout the follow-up period. Therefore, careful consideration of overdiagnosis and its associated consequences is warranted in pediatric patients. To date, modifications to TIRADS for application in pediatric populations have focused on improving diagnostic performance in a balanced manner, not only with increased biopsy cut-off sizes for K-TIRADS 4 or lower nodules to reduce unnecessary biopsies, but also with attempts to lower the biopsy cut-off size for nodules in the highest suspicion category and to incorporate clinical risk factors when determining biopsy thresholds. However, clinical considerations of these modifications should be extended beyond diagnostic performance alone. In pediatric patients, it is also important to comprehensively consider the long-term outcomes related to diagnostic and therapeutic interventions, such as growth and quality of life. Indeed, postthyroidectomy thyroid dysfunction in children may have adverse effects on growth, skeletal maturation, and cognitive development [ ]. Therefore, future modifications to the TIRADS should include further discussions beyond diagnostic performance. Heterogeneity Within Pediatric Thyroid Cancer The cutoff age for pediatric and adult thyroid cancer is currently 18 years, as described in the ATA guidelines [ ]. However, several studies have reported that clinical outcomes for pediatric thyroid cancer vary according to the patient’s age. In particular, thyroid cancers in younger children exhibit more aggressive

outcomes related to diagnostic and therapeutic interventions, such as growth and quality of life. Indeed, postthyroidectomy thyroid dysfunction in children may have adverse effects on growth, skeletal maturation, and cognitive development [ ]. Therefore, future modifications to the TIRADS should include further discussions beyond diagnostic performance. Heterogeneity Within Pediatric Thyroid Cancer The cutoff age for pediatric and adult thyroid cancer is currently 18 years, as described in the ATA guidelines [ ]. However, several studies have reported that clinical outcomes for pediatric thyroid cancer vary according to the patient’s age. In particular, thyroid cancers in younger children exhibit more aggressive features than those in older pediatric populations [ ]. Sugino et al. [ ] analyzed 288 patients under 21 years of age with differentiated thyroid cancer and found that patients younger than 15 years had poorer distant metastasis-free survival compared to those 15 years or older, along with a higher prevalence of tumors larger than 4 cm (45.3% vs. 25.5%; P < 0.01), lymph node metastasis (39.6% vs. 18.7%; P < 0.005), and distant metastasis (22.6% vs. 3.8%; P < 0.001). Similarly, Lazar et al. [ ] reported that, compared to adolescents, pre-pubertal thyroid cancer patients had a higher prevalence of a family history (50.0% vs. 17.5%; P = 0.037), extrathyroidal extension (80.0% vs. 35.5%; P = 0.012), lymph node metastasis (100% vs. 47.0%; P = 0.009), and distant metastasis (70.0% vs. 23.5%; P = 0.009). Liu et al. [ ] also reported that thyroid cancers in patients ≤10 years old showed a higher prevalence of extrathyroidal extension (80.0% vs. 51.4%; P = 0.012), lymph node metastasis (94.3% vs. 74.3%; P = 0.022), and distant metastasis (31.4% vs. 11.4%; P = 0.041), as well as a higher recurrence rate (80.0% vs. 20.0%; P = 0.040), compared to patients older than 10 years. In this context, further clarification of the cut-off between pediatric and adult thyroid cancer, as well as the adoption of a stratified US approach tailored to younger and older pediatric age groups, may be considered in future TIRADS. Toward Incorporation of Molecular Profiles Into Pediatric TIRADS These differences in presentation, even among pediatric thyroid cancers, may be genetically driven. Indeed, BRAF mutations, the most common genetic alteration in adult thyroid cancer, have been reported in 40% of patients younger than 15 years and in 75% of those aged 15–24 years ( P = 0.008) [ ]. Pediatric thyroid cancers are more frequently driven by oncogenic fusions, including RET , NTRK , or ALK [ ]. Tumors associated with these gene fusions often exhibit more invasive behavior, with higher rates of regional and distant metastasis [ ]. The identification of actionable fusions has significant implications for prognosis and targeted therapy selection, as selective inhibitors such as larotrectinib and selpercatinib have shown tumor responses and restoration of radioiodine uptake in fusion-positive pediatric PTCs [ ]. While the pathogenesis underlying tumor behavior in pediatric thyroid cancers is not yet fully understood, accumulating evidence suggests that comprehending their molecular landscape is essential for elucidating disease heterogeneity and, ultimately, for improving clinical management in pediatric thyroid cancer. Consequently, future modifications of K-TIRADS could consider moving beyond US features alone to incorporate molecular profiles. In this approach, US-based risk stratification would guide the indication for molecular testing, while molecular results could be integrated into post-diagnostic risk assessment and treatment decision making. Application of Artificial Intelligence US evaluation of thyroid nodules is inherently limited by operator dependency, leading to substantial interobserver variability in both image acquisition and interpretation [ ]. To mitigate these limitations, various artificial intelligence (AI)–based systems have been developed for thyroid nodule assessment and classification. Notable commercially available systems include AmCAD-UT (AmCad Biomed, Taipei, Taiwan) and S-Detect™ (Samsung Medison Co. Ltd., Seoul, Korea) [ ]. While many studies have shown that experienced physicians typically outperform AI systems [ ], some research indicates comparable or even superior diagnostic performance from AI [ ], particularly when compared to less-experienced radiologists [ ]. AI-based classification has demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity and negative predictive value compared to less-experienced radiologists, suggesting a potential role in reducing false-negative diagnoses among operators with limited experience in thyroid US. In the pediatric population, a pilot study evaluating AI-based thyroid nodule assessment has been reported. Ha et al. [ ] applied a deep learning model trained on adult thyroid US data to 156 pediatric thyroid nodules ( http://cdss.co.kr ). The AI model showed robust performance in differentiating malignant from benign nodules, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranging from 0.913 to 0.929, sensitivities of 78.7% to 89.4%, and specificities of 79.8% to 91.7%. Notably, the AI model achieved a significantly higher area under the curve than radiologist assessments based on either the ACR TI-RADS or K-TIRADS (AI-thyroid vs. ACR TI-RADS, 0.927 vs. 0.831; P = 0.016; vs. K-TIRADS, 0.927

assessment has been reported. Ha et al. [ ] applied a deep learning model trained on adult thyroid US data to 156 pediatric thyroid nodules ( http://cdss.co.kr ). The AI model showed robust performance in differentiating malignant from benign nodules, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranging from 0.913 to 0.929, sensitivities of 78.7% to 89.4%, and specificities of 79.8% to 91.7%. Notably, the AI model achieved a significantly higher area under the curve than radiologist assessments based on either the ACR TI-RADS or K-TIRADS (AI-thyroid vs. ACR TI-RADS, 0.927 vs. 0.831; P = 0.016; vs. K-TIRADS, 0.927 vs. 0.831; P < 0.001). Importantly, while the sensitivity did not differ significantly among methods, the specificity of the AI model was significantly higher than that of K-TIRADS (79.8% vs. 49.5%; P < 0.001). However, it should be noted that the previously reported study was limited to cohorts with available histopathologic confirmation and was retrospective in nature, relying solely on previously acquired US images, raising concerns about the generalizability of these results to real-world clinical practice. Moreover, despite advances in AI-based image interpretation, operator dependency during image acquisition remains, and real-time AI-assisted classification systems capable of providing immediate information during US exams are still limited. Overall, these findings suggest that AI-assisted diagnostic systems may play a role in pediatric thyroid nodule US evaluation and could be integrated into thyroid imaging workflows to enhance objectivity and efficiency, although substantial and robust evidence is required as a prerequisite. Diagnostic Challenges The diffuse sclerosing subtype of PTC is a rare histologic subtype, accounting for about 0.5% to 0.8% of all PTCs [ ]. However, it tends to occur at a younger age than conventional PTC, resulting in a relatively higher frequency in pediatric populations. Indeed, a population-based study found that the diffuse sclerosing subtype of PTC comprised 3.1% of pediatric PTCs but only 0.5% of adult PTCs [ ]. Compared to classic PTC, this subtype is associated with a higher incidence of lymph node and distant metastases and poorer survival [ ], highlighting the importance of early detection. On US, it typically does not present as a well-defined mass but rather as diffuse thyroid enlargement with scattered punctate echogenic foci ( ), which can easily be misinterpreted as diffuse thyroid parenchymal disease [ ]. In response to this diagnostic challenge, the 2021 K-TIRADS specifically classifies the diffuse sclerosing subtype of PTC, characterized by extensive parenchymal punctate echogenic foci without discrete nodules, as K-TIRADS 4 [ ]. By contrast, the AACE/ACE/AME guidelines acknowledge it as a diagnostic challenge but do not specify how it should be categorized on ultrasonography [ ], and the ATA guidelines likewise make no mention of US evaluation [ ]. Therefore, future pediatric-specific US guidelines may need to establish clear ultrasonographic criteria for detecting the diffuse sclerosing subtype of PTC. Another diagnostic challenge concerning pediatric thyroid nodules is intrathyroidal ectopic thymus ( ), a common mimicker of pediatric thyroid nodules. Indeed, Chang et al. [ ] reported that intrathyroidal ectopic thymus was observed in 1% to 3% of pediatric patients. Generally, intrathyroidal ectopic thymus has a smooth margin and appears as a hypoechoic solid nodule with linear or punctate echogenic foci, showing absent or minimal vascularity relative to the surrounding thyroid parenchyma [ ]. Notably, internal punctate echogenic foci may mimic calcifications and should be carefully differentiated. In this regard, the differentiation of intrathyroidal ectopic thymus from a true thyroid nodule can be made by comparing its sonographic appearance with that of a normal mediastinal thymus. Additionally, intrathyroidal ectopic thymus is typically detected at a young age, with the mean age ranging from 8.7 months to 6.3 years, and most cases remain stable or decrease in size on follow-up [ ]. In some cases, the margins become less distinct or the echogenicity may change to hyperechoic. Therefore, when a nodule with punctate echogenic foci is detected in children under 4 years of age—an age group in which thyroid cancer is exceedingly rare [ ]—consideration of ectopic thymus as a differential diagnosis, with follow-up without biopsy, is warranted. Accordingly, future pediatric TIRADS may require clarification regarding the consideration of ectopic thymus in young children. CONCLUSION Pediatric thyroid cancer is rare but shows clinical features distinct from those of adult thyroid cancer, indicating that pediatric thyroid nodules require a specific management strategy. Recent modifications of the K-TIRADS in 2021 include pediatric-specific biopsy cut-offs and risk-adapted considerations that have improved diagnostic accuracy compared with the previous version. Therefore, the 2021 K-TIRADS may be an appropriate framework available at present for the management of pediatric thyroid nodules. However, important challenges remain in the pediatric population, including age-related heterogeneity, pediatric-specific diagnostic mimickers, and the need for further validation and integration of molecular- and AI-based approaches. These challenges need to be addressed in future studies.

chunks.content: Introduction Thyroid nodules are a common disease, and their detection rate has gradually increased with the application of high-resolution ultrasound in recent years, with a trend toward younger age at diagnosis [ , ]. However, the vast majority of thyroid nodules are pathologically confirmed to be benign, with only 7–15% being malignant [ ]. The key point in the diagnosis and management of thyroid nodules is the differentiation between benign and malignant lesions. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNA) is regarded as the gold standard for the preoperative diagnosis of thyroid nodules; however, it is an invasive procedure that increases patients’ psychological and economic burdens [ ]. Additionally, some patients experience significant psychological distress due to the inability to confirm the pathological nature of their nodules, leading to numerous unnecessary diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Ultrasonography (US) examination is characterized by simplicity, real-time imaging, non-invasiveness, and high cost-effectiveness; thus, it serves as the primary imaging modality for evaluating thyroid nodules [ , ]. The accurate detection rate of thyroid nodules using US has been reported to range from 81.5% to 99.1% [ ]. Among the ultrasound findings of thyroid nodules, calcification is recognized as a critical sign with high diagnostic significance; however, comprehensive evaluation is required based on its specific type and size, as the correlation between different calcification subtypes and malignant risk differs. For instance, macrocalcifications (e.g., complete annular calcification and coarse calcification) are more prevalent in benign nodules, whereas specific subtypes of microcalcifications (e.g., psammoma bodies [PBs], which are highly suggestive of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC)) confer greater predictive value for malignant lesions [ – ]. Numerous prior studies have demonstrated that the incidence of microcalcifications is significantly higher in malignant nodules than in benign counterparts [ ]. Consequently, among all calcification subtypes, microcalcifications have garnered the greatest attention in clinical and research settings [ ]. However, the overall clinical significance of calcifications in differentiating benign from malignant thyroid nodules remains incompletely elucidated [ , ]. One of the core reasons is the lack of a unified standard for radiologists to define various bright spots (e.g., microcalcifications, colloid crystals, backwall enhancement, or comet tail artifacts) on ultrasound images, which often hinders precise correlation with pathological calcifications [ – ]. For instance, structures identified as “microcalcifications” on ultrasound may not only represent pathologically defined PBs but also correspond to benign components such as concentrated colloid crystals and stromal microcalcifications. Additionally, they must be differentiated from benign artifacts, including backwall enhancement and comet tail artifacts. This often makes it difficult to accurately identify pathologically defined microcalcifications (i.e., PBs) via ultrasound in clinical practice. Consequently, accurately distinguishing the nature of these bright spots has emerged as a key challenge in thyroid ultrasound diagnosis [ ]. Therefore, there is an urgent need for a more objective method to explore and utilize the malignant predictive value of “calcifications” in ultrasound images of thyroid nodules. In recent years, deep learning (DL) has achieved remarkable success in the field of image classification by learning patterns directly from raw data through neural networks [ ]. Multiple studies on thyroid nodule differentiation using DL have demonstrated that DL methods can effectively learn diverse features from thyroid nodules, assist radiologists in improving diagnostic capabilities, and reduce unnecessary FNA procedures [ – ]. However, DL research focusing on “calcification”—a critical imaging feature—remains limited. Traditional DL models largely rely on the input of single global features of nodules, with local calcification features not incorporated separately. This may result in insufficient recognition of subtle calcification features associated with malignancy. Additionally, data acquired from different centers and ultrasound devices exhibits heterogeneity, which imposes heightened demands on the generalization ability of models. Wang et al. [ ] aimed to detect and quantify calcifications in thyroid nodules based on ultrasound images and further investigate the value of “calcification” on ultrasound images in predicting the risk of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in PTC. Our team has also conducted relevant studies previously [ – ], in which preliminary exploration of “calcification” features in ultrasound images of nodules was performed, providing early evidence for imaging analysis in this field. Consequently, an innovative “calcification”-enhanced DL approach is proposed in this study. Based on large-scale multicenter ultrasound data, a dual-branch DL model (DL AM−CFF ) was developed to automatically detect thyroid nodules and their associated calcifications, with calcification-related features automatically extracted and modeled. The model leverages two separate branches to learn global imaging features of nodules and local calcification features, respectively. An attention mechanism is incorporated during the fusion stage to dynamically weight high-value features (e.g., calcification location and morphology), thereby enhancing the correlation between the two feature types, effectively suppressing noise interference, and more efficiently capturing interactive information between calcification patterns and nodule backgrounds. This facilitates the accurate identification of subtle calcification structures highly associated with malignant risk. Additionally, ultrasound data

(DL AM−CFF ) was developed to automatically detect thyroid nodules and their associated calcifications, with calcification-related features automatically extracted and modeled. The model leverages two separate branches to learn global imaging features of nodules and local calcification features, respectively. An attention mechanism is incorporated during the fusion stage to dynamically weight high-value features (e.g., calcification location and morphology), thereby enhancing the correlation between the two feature types, effectively suppressing noise interference, and more efficiently capturing interactive information between calcification patterns and nodule backgrounds. This facilitates the accurate identification of subtle calcification structures highly associated with malignant risk. Additionally, ultrasound data from multiple centers and devices was incorporated in this study to introduce data heterogeneity, thereby further improving the model’s generalization ability. Through the objective extraction and fusion analysis of “calcifications” via DL, this study aims to improve the accuracy of differentiating benign from malignant thyroid nodules and provide a more reliable and objective diagnostic aid for clinical practice. Materials and methods This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhejiang Cancer Hospital. For the retrospectively collected ultrasound images, a waiver of informed consent was granted (IRB-2024-580 (IIT)). Study design and datasets This was a multicenter retrospective diagnostic study that utilized an ultrasound image dataset from 3 hospitals in China, collected between January 2014 and March 2024. Patients with ultrasound-confirmed thyroid nodules and clearly documented definitive clinical diagnoses of benign or malignant status in the electronic medical record system were included. This definitive clinical diagnosis was established based on clinical pathways, either via postoperative histopathology or Bethesda II/VI FNA cytology. All preoperative ultrasound images were initially included, but low-quality or low-resolution images were excluded following screening. In this study, all thyroid nodule images from each center were acquired using various devices manufactured by multiple vendors, including Philips, Toshiba, GE Healthcare, and Siemens. A two-stage DL model (DL AM−CFF ) based on a calcification enhancement strategy was proposed for the differential diagnosis of benign and malignant thyroid nodules with calcifications. The overall workflow of the model is presented in Fig. . In the first stage, the thyroid nodule region and its internal calcification regions were extracted using a semantic segmentation method, and two independent regions of interest (ROIs) were constructed based on these segmented regions. In the second stage, a dual-branch convolutional neural network (CNN) was designed to extract features from the calcification regions and the entire nodule regions separately. Final classification decisions were made through feature fusion and an attention mechanism. It is important to emphasize that the automatic extraction of calcification regions in this study was not intended to independently classify calcifications or determine their histological properties, but rather to provide locally high-risk features with diagnostic value for differentiating benign from malignant nodules. Since the imaging interpretation of calcifications cannot be separated from the overall structure and context of the nodule, and the diagnosis of nodule benignancy or malignancy also relies on the integrated information of both, the entire nodule ROI was simultaneously extracted, and the two types of features were fused in subsequent network layers for the final benign-malignant classification. For the development and testing of the DL AM−CFF model (for differentiating benign and malignant thyroid nodules), a total of 11,634 ultrasound images from 6886 thyroid nodules were included in this study from the ultrasound image dataset. Ultrasound images were divided into mutually independent training, validation, and test sets at a ratio of 7:1 :2 based on the unique ID of each nodule. All nodules from the same patient were assigned to the same dataset. Stratified sampling based on the benign-malignant ratio was employed to ensure balanced distribution of baseline characteristics across all datasets, with results presented in Table . Calcification and nodule region segmentation First, a publicly available thyroid nodule segmentation network based on the Swin-Unet architecture was used for the initial segmentation of thyroid nodules in ultrasound images [ ]. This network has demonstrated favorable performance across multiple medical image segmentation tasks and is particularly suitable for lesion regions with ill-defined boundaries or complex structures. Precise localization of nodule regions was achieved using its pre-trained weights. Building on the nodule segmentation results, potential intranodular calcifications were further identified, and a calcification segmentation method based on local gray-level thresholds was proposed. Calcifications in ultrasound images typically appear as local hyperechoic regions; however, their absolute gray-level values are susceptible to variations in imaging parameters and equipment. To address this issue, an adaptive thresholding algorithm based on intranodular gray-level distribution was proposed. This algorithm first calculates the quartiles of pixel intensity within each nodule region, followed by the determination of a calcification identification threshold based on the third quartile and interquartile range (IQR). This strategy effectively mitigates interference from inter-image gray-level variations and focuses on identifying echo points within each nodule that are significantly brighter relative to their surrounding

gray-level thresholds was proposed. Calcifications in ultrasound images typically appear as local hyperechoic regions; however, their absolute gray-level values are susceptible to variations in imaging parameters and equipment. To address this issue, an adaptive thresholding algorithm based on intranodular gray-level distribution was proposed. This algorithm first calculates the quartiles of pixel intensity within each nodule region, followed by the determination of a calcification identification threshold based on the third quartile and interquartile range (IQR). This strategy effectively mitigates interference from inter-image gray-level variations and focuses on identifying echo points within each nodule that are significantly brighter relative to their surrounding background; these points are preliminarily designated as potential calcification regions. To further improve the specificity of calcification segmentation, morphological processing was applied to the initially extracted potential regions to remove scattered noise points and preserve the morphology of clinically relevant calcifications. Finally, based on the nodule segmentation results and calcification segmentation results, the overall nodule ROI (224 × 224 pixels) and calcification region ROI (96 × 96 pixels) were cropped separately and used as inputs for the second-stage classification network. Design of the dual-branch classification network A dual-branch structure was employed in the second stage to process the calcification ROI and overall nodule ROI separately, enabling the simultaneous capture of micro-scale calcification morphological features and macro-scale nodule structural features. For the calcification feature extraction branch, the cropped calcification region images (96 × 96 × 3) were used as input. Given the typically small size and diverse morphologies of calcification regions, the network was required to have strong local feature reuse and detail capture capabilities. Consequently, DenseNet121 was selected as the backbone network. DenseNet facilitates feature reuse and enhances gradient flow through its dense connection mechanism, making it particularly suitable for feature extraction of microcalcifications. Subsequently, an UpSampling2D layer and Conv2D layer were further incorporated to expand the feature maps to higher resolutions, restoring detailed information that might have been lost during downsampling. Finally, a multi-head self-attention module was designed to model long-range dependencies within calcification regions, emphasizing important features and suppressing redundant information. For the nodule global feature extraction branch, the input was the overall nodule ROI (224 × 224 × 3), which was designed to extract macro-scale features of nodules, such as overall morphology, edge regularity, and internal echogenicity. The Extreme Inception (Xception) network was selected as the backbone network for this branch. Xception [ ] is a deep convolutional neural network proposed by Chollet. Its core innovation lies in the replacement of traditional convolutions with depthwise separable convolutions, which reduces the number of parameters while preserving robust feature representation capabilities. Notably, it is particularly well-suited for medium-scale image classification tasks. Its multi-scale feature extraction capability also contributes to capturing structural information of nodules at different levels. The features output by the two branches were concatenated to form a combined feature representation. This fused feature not only contains local detailed information of the calcification region but also integrates the global contextual information of the entire nodule. Subsequently, the fused features were downsampled using a global average pooling layer to reduce the risk of overfitting, followed by connection to fully connected layers for outputting the final benign/malignant probabilities. A Sigmoid activation function was used in the classification layer to achieve binary classification output. Training details and implementation The ultrasound images used for training, validation, and testing of the DL AM−CFF model in this study were randomly partitioned from the ultrasound image dataset at a predefined ratio. For fair comparison, the DL AM−CFF model and four classical CNN models (Xception, InceptionResNetV2, DenseNet121, and ResNet50) were all trained, validated, and tested using the same training, validation, and test sets. Additionally, a single-branch classification network (DL CFF ) that retains only the nodule global feature extraction branch was designed to validate the effectiveness of the calcification feature extraction branch. Furthermore, all models were implemented on the Ubuntu 20.04 operating system using the Keras 2.5.0 and TensorFlow 2.5.0 frameworks. The host machine used was equipped with an Intel ® Core™ i9-13900 K @ 3.0 GHz and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti 8 GB GPU. During the training process, the batch size was set to 16, and the training was conducted for 60 epochs. Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using the Python language. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were used as evaluation metrics in this study. Additionally, 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used to estimate the ranges of these values. Comparisons of AUC values between models were conducted using the DeLong test. The F1-score was used to comprehensively evaluate the precision and recall of model classification, while the Kappa coefficient was used to quantitatively analyze the classification agreement between model diagnostic results and the pathological gold

Statistical analysis All statistical analyses were performed using the Python language. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) were used as evaluation metrics in this study. Additionally, 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used to estimate the ranges of these values. Comparisons of AUC values between models were conducted using the DeLong test. The F1-score was used to comprehensively evaluate the precision and recall of model classification, while the Kappa coefficient was used to quantitatively analyze the classification agreement between model diagnostic results and the pathological gold standard. A two-tailed P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Patient characteristics A total of 6886 thyroid nodule cases were retrospectively collected from 3 hospitals in this study. Among these cases, 4433 were benign nodules (64.38%) and 2453 were malignant nodules (35.62%). The training set consisted of 8134 images from 4820 cases, the validation set comprised 1187 images from 688 cases, and the test set included 2313 images from 1378 cases. The baseline characteristics of the cases are presented in Table . Predictive accuracy of DL models for discriminating malignant and benign nodules The performance of six DL models—including DL AM−CFF , DL CFF , Xception, InceptionResNetV2, DenseNet121, and ResNet50—in the classification task was compared in this study. Table presents the diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity of each DL model in the test set. Figure illustrates the confusion matrices for benign-malignant thyroid nodule classification of each model, which further reveal the specific distribution characteristics of classification errors. DL CFF performs classification solely based on nodule features. Its diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity were 0.846 (95% CI: 0.824, 0.868), 0.844 (95% CI: 0.807, 0.881), and 0.847 (95% CI: 0.820, 0.875), respectively. As observed from the confusion matrix results, 58 false negatives (missed diagnosis rate: 15.6%) and 101 false positives (misdiagnosis rate: 15.3%) were reported for DL CFF . The diagnostic performance of DL AM−CFF was improved by integrating nodule features with calcification features, optimized through the introduction of an attention mechanism. Its diagnostic accuracy reached 0.864 (95% CI: 0.843, 0.884), with a sensitivity of 0.863 (95% CI: 0.827, 0.898) and specificity of 0.864 (95% CI: 0.838, 0.890). As observed from the confusion matrix results, only 51 false negatives (missed diagnosis rate: 13.7%) and 88 false positives (misdiagnosis rate: 13.3%) were reported for DL AM−CFF , with both the number of missed malignant cases and misdiagnosed benign cases lower than those of all comparative models. Among other commonly used models, Xception achieved an accuracy of 0.821 (95% CI: 0.798, 0.845), sensitivity of 0.815 (95% CI: 0.778, 0.852), and specificity of 0.826 (95% CI: 0.799, 0.853). InceptionResNetV2 exhibited an accuracy of 0.793 (95% CI: 0.768, 0.818), sensitivity of 0.789 (95% CI: 0.751, 0.827), and specificity of 0.796 (95% CI: 0.769, 0.823). DenseNet121 and ResNet50 demonstrated poorer performance, with ResNet50 achieving the lowest accuracy of 0.746 (95% CI: 0.720, 0.773), a sensitivity of 0.682 (95% CI: 0.635, 0.729), and a specificity of 0.769 (95% CI: 0.737, 0.801). Additionally, 118 false negatives (missed diagnosis rate: 31.8%) were reported for ResNet50, indicating an extremely high clinical risk of missed diagnosis. In summary, the confusion matrix of DL AM−CFF is consistent with its quantitative metrics, demonstrating that DL AM−CFF achieves the best performance in terms of overall classification accuracy and malignant nodule detection. Receiver-operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis of DL models The ROC curves and AUC values of each model are presented in Fig. . DL AM−CFF exhibited the best performance, with an AUC of 0.925 (95% CI: 0.909, 0.941), which indicated the strongest comprehensive ability to differentiate benign from malignant thyroid nodules. DL CFF ranked second, with an AUC of 0.905 (95% CI: 0.887, 0.923). A DeLong test was conducted to compare the AUC values of the two models, with the difference identified as statistically significant ( P < 0.05; Fig. ). This result confirmed that the overall discriminative performance of DL AM−CFF was significantly superior to that of DL CFF . Among other commonly used models, the AUC of Xception was 0.883 (95% CI: 0.863, 0.903). For InceptionResNetV2 and DenseNet121, the AUC values were 0.855 (95% CI: 0.834, 0.877) and 0.822 (95% CI: 0.799, 0.845), respectively. ResNet50 exhibited the weakest performance, with an AUC of only 0.797 (95% CI: 0.772, 0.821). All these AUC values were significantly lower than those of DL AM−CFF and DL CFF (both developed in this study), with the differences deemed statistically significant ( P < 0.05). Visualization of model attention regions Grad-CAM heatmaps were used to visualize the key regions of interest for the model during decision-making (Fig. ). Red-yellow regions indicate a higher degree of model attention. For malignant nodules (Panels a–d, e–h), the DL AM–CFF model consistently focused on malignant ultrasound signs associated with thyroid cancer. For

All these AUC values were significantly lower than those of DL AM−CFF and DL CFF (both developed in this study), with the differences deemed statistically significant ( P < 0.05). Visualization of model attention regions Grad-CAM heatmaps were used to visualize the key regions of interest for the model during decision-making (Fig. ). Red-yellow regions indicate a higher degree of model attention. For malignant nodules (Panels a–d, e–h), the DL AM–CFF model consistently focused on malignant ultrasound signs associated with thyroid cancer. For nodules with microcalcifications (Panels a–d), the model focused primarily on intranodular microcalcifications and the surrounding irregular hypoechoic structures. For calcification-free nodules with prominent malignant features (Panels e–h), the model focused on regions with ill-defined borders and internal heterogeneity. For benign nodules (Panels i–l, m–p), the heatmaps exhibited a low-intensity, diffuse activation pattern. In calcification-free benign nodules (Panels i–l), the model only showed mild attention to uniform, regular internal echoes. In nodules with macrocalcifications (Panels m–p), the model reduced its attention to macrocalcifications and their acoustic shadows, concentrating activation on the periphery of calcifications rather than the nodule parenchyma—this is consistent with their low malignant potential. Discussion The results of this study showed that the “calcification”-enhanced DL model (DL AM−CFF ) exhibited the best performance in thyroid nodule classification tasks, with an AUC of 0.925, a sensitivity of 0.863, and a specificity of 0.864. This performance was significantly superior to that of DL CFF (which relies solely on nodule features) and other classical models, and this advantage was closely associated with the model’s design that integrates overall nodule features with “calcification” features. Clinically, the interpretation of calcifications cannot be separated from the overall information of the nodule, and the diagnostic significance of calcifications depends on their location, distribution within the nodule, and accompanying imaging features. It was observed that relying solely on local features of calcification regions is insufficient to support accurate benign-malignant differentiation, while relying solely on overall structural information of the nodule fails to capture key details such as microcalcifications. Therefore, this study proposes treating the calcification ROI as a supplementary feature that provides local high-risk cues. Through fusion with overall nodule features via an attention mechanism, enhanced representation of malignant signs is achieved, which constitutes the “calcification”-enhanced nodule risk assessment strategy. A workflow framework of “nodule segmentation-calcification segmentation-dual-branch feature extraction” was employed in this study. This framework first precisely segmented thyroid nodule regions from raw ultrasound images, followed by the identification and extraction of intranodular calcifications, thereby eliminating interference from glandular tissue and surrounding structures for subsequent feature extraction. Notably, the integration of a dual-branch structure and an attention mechanism facilitates addressing the challenges associated with identifying thyroid microcalcifications, including their small size, scattered distribution, and propensity for confusion with colloid and other structures. Therefore, compared with the DL CFF model (which does not incorporate calcification features), DL AM−CFF learns the overall nodule context and local calcification details in parallel. By enhancing key calcification features with dynamic weights, it not only reduces the omission of microcalcifications but also suppresses non-specific noise—this is the key reason for the simultaneous improvement in the model’s sensitivity and specificity. Furthermore, Grad-CAM visualizations further confirmed that the regions attended to by the DL AM–CFF model are consistent with clinically high-risk features, including microcalcifications, intranodular heterogeneity, and border abnormalities—thus supporting the interpretability and clinical acceptability of the DL AM–CFF model. Thyroid nodules with microcalcifications are associated with a higher malignant risk and frequently indicate malignant lesions, such as PTC. In contrast, macrocalcifications and marginal arc-shaped calcifications are mostly associated with benign lesions (e.g., nodular goiter, adenoma) and have a lower malignant probability. However, in clinical practice, accurate identification of calcification types still faces several challenges: microcalcifications are prone to misdiagnosis due to their small size and easy confusion with colloid crystals and artifacts; mixed calcifications are difficult to differentiate due to their complex morphological feature; subtle features are hard to quantify; and the consistency of manual diagnosis is low due to variations in radiologists’ experience and equipment differences. Park et al. [ ] analyzed ultrasound findings of 854 thyroid nodules with macrocalcifications and found that the presence of interrupted calcifications, irregular thickness, and soft tissue margins was associated with malignancy in thyroid nodules with macrocalcifications. Chen et al. [ ] reported that radiologists demonstrated significantly insufficient diagnostic consistency in differentiating between calcifications and colloid within echogenic foci of thyroid nodules. Specifically, the mean Kappa value was only 0.2122 in the echogenic foci subgroup and only 0.5853 in the punctate echogenic foci subgroup. This finding indicates that manual interpretation has significant subjective variability in the differentiation of such subtle imaging features. Furthermore, DL-based auxiliary assessment for calcification features of thyroid nodules has not yet been

that the presence of interrupted calcifications, irregular thickness, and soft tissue margins was associated with malignancy in thyroid nodules with macrocalcifications. Chen et al. [ ] reported that radiologists demonstrated significantly insufficient diagnostic consistency in differentiating between calcifications and colloid within echogenic foci of thyroid nodules. Specifically, the mean Kappa value was only 0.2122 in the echogenic foci subgroup and only 0.5853 in the punctate echogenic foci subgroup. This finding indicates that manual interpretation has significant subjective variability in the differentiation of such subtle imaging features. Furthermore, DL-based auxiliary assessment for calcification features of thyroid nodules has not yet been fully explored, making it difficult to accurately analyze the malignant risk associated with this critical feature. The effectiveness of DL in the auxiliary diagnosis of thyroid nodules with echogenic foci has been demonstrated in our previous studies [ , ]. However, these studies utilized datasets from only one or two centers, with a limited sample size, and failed to fully cover the diverse calcification subtypes and imaging heterogeneity encountered in clinical practice. Consequently, they may be insufficient for evaluating the generalization performance of models across multiple centers, devices, and diverse populations. In light of this, a DL AM−CFF model that integrates features from different imaging devices and covers various calcification types was developed in this study based on a multicenter ultrasound dataset cohort. This model is designed to achieve accurate identification and benign/malignant classification of thyroid nodules by fusing calcification features, provide objective evidence for the assessment of thyroid nodule malignancy through the analysis of calcification features, and enhance the clinical utility of DL in calcification-related diagnosis of thyroid nodules. The results showed that the DL AM−CFF model, which fuses nodule and intranodular calcification features, exhibited good performance in thyroid nodule classification tasks and has the potential to provide reliable auxiliary diagnosis for radiologists. This study has the following limitations: First, the included malignant nodules are predominantly classic PTC, with a small sample size of rare subtypes such as follicular carcinoma and medullary carcinoma. This may compromise the model’s performance in identifying such nodules and limit the contributory value of calcification features across different pathological subtypes; Second, the model was constructed based on static ultrasound images, which can only capture information from a single frame and fail to acquire multi-planar morphology, mobility, hemodynamic features of nodules, and their relationships with adjacent structures during dynamic scanning. This results in discrepancies from real clinical diagnostic scenarios; Finally, calcification segmentation was not quantitatively evaluated due to the absence of standardized annotations, although ablation results indirectly support its value. Future research will advance in three aspects: First, prospective multicenter studies will be conducted to expand the sample size of rare subtypes such as follicular carcinoma and medullary carcinoma, and subgroup analyses will be performed to validate the model’s generalization ability; Second, dynamic ultrasound videos will be incorporated to capture richer spatial features, and a spatial-feature-based DL framework will be developed to align with clinical dynamic diagnostic workflows; Finally, standardized pixel-level calcification annotations will be incorporated to enable quantitative evaluation of the segmentation module and comparison with existing segmentation networks. Conclusion In conclusion, this study demonstrated that the “calcification”-enhanced DL approach significantly outperforms strategies relying solely on single nodule features in the differentiation of benign and malignant thyroid nodules, and can effectively improve diagnostic accuracy. This approach has demonstrated unique advantages in identifying calcification-related malignant features and holds promise for development as a reliable auxiliary tool for the accurate clinical diagnosis of thyroid nodules in the future.

documents.title: ATA Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Hyperthyroidism Graves Disease

chunks.content: Introduction Graves’ disease is an autoimmune disorder characterised by the presence of thyroid-stimulating antibodies, which cause thyrotoxicosis and diffuse goitre. In some cases, the disease can also lead to orbitopathy or dermopathy. Treatment options include antithyroid drugs (ATDs), radioactive iodine (RAI) and thyroidectomy [ ]. Although ATDs and RAI are commonly used for initial treatment [ , ], total thyroidectomy is recommended for patients with large goitre, intolerance or resistance to ATDs, moderate-to-severe orbitopathy, suspicious thyroid nodules or concomitant hyperparathyroidism [ ]. The American Thyroid Association, the European Thyroid Association and the American Association of Endocrine Surgeons are among the endocrine societies that recommend achieving a euthyroid state preoperatively to minimise the risk of thyroid storm, a rare but potentially fatal complication of uncontrolled hyperthyroidism [ – ]. However, the evidence supporting this long-standing recommendation remains limited [ ]. In contemporary thyroid surgery, thyroid storm and postoperative acute renal insufficiency are considered exceedingly rare. The incidence of thyroid storm is reported to be nearly zero when preoperative thyroid function is adequately controlled. In contrast, the incidence in patients with poorly controlled hyperthyroidism has not been well quantified, largely due to heterogeneity in disease severity and definitions. Furthermore, achieving complete biochemical normalization is often challenging in real-world clinical practice because of intolerance to antithyroid drugs, adverse effects, refractory hormone levels, nonadherence, and urgent surgical indications [ – ]. Consequently, surgery may need to proceed even when thyroid function is not fully controlled. Therapeutic plasma exchange can be used as a last resort in emergency settings, but its invasiveness and limited availability restrict its routine use [ , ]. The mechanism underlying thyroid storm is thought to involve excessive hormone release triggered by manipulation of the thyroid gland, compounded by the physiological stress of surgery. Additionally, patients with severe hyperthyroidism may exhibit relative adrenal insufficiency due to the increased metabolism of corticosteroids, which can exacerbate the stress response [ , ]. Despite these concerns, recent studies suggest that total thyroidectomy can be safely performed in patients with active thyrotoxicosis, particularly in high-volume centers with experienced surgical teams [ – ]. Advances in modern surgical and anesthetic techniques, including total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA), advanced hemostatic devices, and intraoperative nerve monitoring (IONM), are thought to reduce perioperative stress and enhance safety, even in hyperthyroid patients [ – ]. Consequently, surgery is now more readily performed in patients with incomplete biochemical control. However, physiological evidence comparing the perioperative endocrine responses of euthyroid and hyperthyroid Graves’ disease patients is limited. Few studies have examined intraoperative changes in thyroid hormones and adrenal function in relation to preoperative thyroid status, highlighting the need for detailed endocrine assessments during the perioperative period. This prospective cohort study aimed to investigate the perioperative endocrine changes focusing on thyroid hormones and cortisol in patients undergoing total thyroidectomy for Graves’ disease. By comparing patients with euthyroid and hyperthyroid status at the time of surgery, we sought to clarify the physiological response to surgical stress under different hormonal conditions and evaluate the clinical safety of surgery in patients with uncontrolled hyperthyroidism. Methods Ethical considerations This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Yamashita Thyroid Hospital (Approval No. 2022-13). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Study population and design We prospectively enrolled 39 consecutive patients with Graves’ disease who underwent total thyroidectomy at our institution between June 2022 and May 2023. Severe hepatic or renal dysfunction was predefined as an exclusion criterion; however, no patients met these conditions during the study period. The primary indication for surgery was poorly controlled hyperthyroidism under medical treatment ( n = 17), including six patients who experienced adverse reactions to antithyroid medications. Preoperative physiological parameters, including heart rate, blood pressure, and body temperature, were monitored and confirmed to be within clinically acceptable ranges in all patients prior to surgery. Preoperative management included antithyroid drugs (methimazole or propylthiouracil), potassium iodide (KI), and β-adrenergic blockers, either alone or in combination. Patients were classified as hyperthyroid (HT, n = 17) if preoperative FT3 and/or FT4 levels exceeded the upper limit of the institutional reference range at the time of surgery, despite ongoing antithyroid drug therapy. Patients with thyroid hormone levels within the reference ranges were classified as euthyroid (ET, n = 22). Perioperative protocol and blood sampling Three blood samples were collected from each patient at the following time points: T0 (the day before surgery), T1 (after thyroid removal), and T2 (8:00 a.m. on the first postoperative day). Serum thyroid hormones, cortisol, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and biochemical markers were measured. The mean interval between thyroidectomy and postoperative blood sampling was 17.1 ± 2.0 h (range: 12.8–21.0 h).
