therapy. Patients with thyroid hormone levels within the reference ranges were classified as euthyroid (ET, n = 22). Perioperative protocol and blood sampling Three blood samples were collected from each patient at the following time points: T0 (the day before surgery), T1 (after thyroid removal), and T2 (8:00 a.m. on the first postoperative day). Serum thyroid hormones, cortisol, parathyroid hormone (PTH), and biochemical markers were measured. The mean interval between thyroidectomy and postoperative blood sampling was 17.1 ± 2.0 h (range: 12.8–21.0 h). Anesthesia and surgical procedure The anesthesia protocol was the same for all patients. The patients were under general anesthesia with TIVA during surgery. Remifentanil 0.2–2.0 µg/kg/min and propofol 3–5 µg/mL in blood concentration by target-controlled infusion were used to induce anesthesia, and muscle relaxation was obtained with rocuronium 0.6 mg/kg, followed by electromyography (EMG) endotracheal tube intubation. At the beginning of the surgery, muscle relaxation was antagonized with sugammadex 2 mg/kg to allow IONM with an EMG endotracheal tube, and anesthesia was maintained with remifentanil 0.2-0.5 μg /kg/min and propofol 2–4 µg/ml. At the end of surgery, fentanyl 100 µg and acetaminophen 1,000 mg were administered for postoperative pain control. All surgeries were performed by five experienced endocrine surgeons. All patients underwent total thyroidectomy using the Thunderbeat Open Fine Jaw (Olympus, Japan) or Harmonic Focus (Ethicon, Johnson and Johnson, Cincinnati, OH, USA. Vessels were carefully ligated prior to gland mobilization to prevent hormone release. The thyroid glands were removed by extracapsular dissection with IONM [ ] of the recurrent laryngeal nerves, external branches of the laryngeal nerve, and preservation of the parathyroid glands. Levothyroxine replacement therapy was initiated on the day following surgery unless the patient exhibited extreme hyperthyroidism (where Free T3 is three times or more the upper limit of normal). Laboratory parameters Serum levels of alkaline phosphatase (ALP; normal range, 38–113 IU/L), total calcium (Ca) (8.8–10.1 mg/dL), and albumin (3.4–4.8 g/L) were measured using routine automated procedures. The Ca level was calculated using the formula: [Ca concentration (mg/dL) + 0.8 × (4 − albumin (g/dL))]. Free thyroxine (0.9–1.7 ng/dL), free triiodothyronine (2.3–4.3 pg/mL), thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH, 0.5–5.0 mU/L), PTH (15–65 pg/mL), cortisol, and anti-TSH receptor antibody (TRAb) (< 2 IU/L) levels were determined using an electrochemiluminescence immunoassay (COBAS 8000 e801 analyzer, Roche Diagnostics, Indianapolis, IN, USA). Statistical analysis Data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Statistical differences between the two study groups were assessed using the t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, depending on the distribution. Biochemical changes before and after surgery were analyzed using paired t-tests for parametric values and Wilcoxon signed-rank test for nonparametric values. Cross-tabulated data were analyzed using Fisher’s exact probability test. The correlations were tested using Spearman’s rank correlation coefficients. All statistical analyses were performed using JMP software (version 17.0; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). Differences were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05. Results The clinical and biochemical characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table . The HT and ET groups showed no significant differences in terms of age, sex distribution, operative time, blood loss, or resected thyroid weight. However, serum levels of free triiodothyronine, free thyroxine, TRAb, and ALP were significantly higher in the HT group, while TSH levels were significantly lower. The duration of preoperative treatment was significantly longer in the ET group. The use of β-blockers, KI, and corticosteroids was also significantly more frequent in the HT group. Changes in the biochemical data of patients who underwent total thyroidectomy are shown in Tables , and . In all cases, the serum level of free triiodothyronine at T1 was significantly lower than that at T0 ( p < 0.0001), whereas that of free thyroxine did not change significantly (Table ). Serum free triiodothyronine levels at T1 showed a significant decrease in both groups (8.21 ± 4.51 pg/mL to 6.19 ± 3.65 pg/mL in the HT group and 2.78 ± 0.47 pg/mL to 2.44 ± 0.48 pg/mL in the ET group), with no cases of elevation in the HT group (Tables and ). Thirteen of the seventeen patients (76.5%) in the HT group had serum free triiodothyronine concentrations within the reference range the following morning. Serum free thyroxine levels at T1 post-thyroidectomy exhibited no significant difference in the HT group and a slight significant increase in the ET group (2.02 ± 1.13 ng/dL to 2.06 ± 1.19 ng/dL in the HT group and 0.92 ± 0.19 pg/mL to 0.97 ± 0.21 ng/dL in the ET group, p < 0.001) (Tables and ). The percentage of free triiodothyronine levels at T2 vs. T1 showed a significant negative correlation with the levels of preoperative free triiodothyronine (Spearman’s ρ = -0.692, p < 0.0001) (Fig. ). One patient with preoperative hypothyroidism (free triiodothyronine: 3.32 pg/mL and free thyroxine: 0.5 ng/dL) was excluded from the above

exhibited no significant difference in the HT group and a slight significant increase in the ET group (2.02 ± 1.13 ng/dL to 2.06 ± 1.19 ng/dL in the HT group and 0.92 ± 0.19 pg/mL to 0.97 ± 0.21 ng/dL in the ET group, p < 0.001) (Tables and ). The percentage of free triiodothyronine levels at T2 vs. T1 showed a significant negative correlation with the levels of preoperative free triiodothyronine (Spearman’s ρ = -0.692, p < 0.0001) (Fig. ). One patient with preoperative hypothyroidism (free triiodothyronine: 3.32 pg/mL and free thyroxine: 0.5 ng/dL) was excluded from the above analysis because he received 200 µg of L-thyroxine on the day before and early morning of the day of surgery. While preoperative cortisol levels were comparable between the groups (HT group: 6.94 ± 3.84 µg/dL, ET group: 8.35 ± 2.62 µg/dL, p = 0.204), levels in the HT group were significantly lower than in the ET group at T1 (HT group: 1.95 ± 1.15 µg/dL vs. ET group: 3.61 ± 1.69 µg/dL, p < 0.005). However, this difference was not significant the next morning (HT group: 13.46 ± 5.91 µg/dL, ET group: 12.23 ± 6.42 µg/dL, p = 0.108) (Fig. ). Four patients in the HT group, who received dexamethasone preoperatively, were excluded from the data analysis. Serum thyroglobulin levels were significantly increased after thyroidectomy compared to preoperative levels (Tables and ), but there was no significant difference between the HT and ET groups (4717 ± 6388 ng/mL vs., 3412 ± 3492 ng/mL p = 0.944). The extracted thyroid weight did not correlate with the preoperative serum thyroglobulin levels. However, it showed a significant positive correlation with the postoperative serum thyroglobulin levels after extraction (Spearman’s ρ = 0.465, p < 0.005). There were no significant differences in the physiological data regarding body temperature, blood pressure, and pulse rate during general anesthesia and the morning after surgery between the HT and ET groups (Supplementary Table 1). No significant differences in the use of remifentanil, propofol, or vasoactive drugs during surgery were found between the two groups (Supplementary Table 2). Supplementary Table 1 Physiological parameters during anesthesia and the morning after surgery. Additionally, postoperative complications, including serum Ca-related results, did not differ between the two groups (Table ). No permanent recurrent nerve palsies were observed, and six patients who received a low dose of active vitamin D (0.5–1.0 µg alfacalcidol) at their final postoperative visit had PTH levels of 37.9 ± 21.1 (20–78 pg/mL). Discussion Our findings are consistent with emerging evidence suggesting that total thyroidectomy can be safely performed on patients who have not achieved full biochemical control. Recent large-scale and meta-analytic studies have demonstrated that hyperthyroid patients do not experience higher rates of postoperative complications than euthyroid patients. These findings reinforce the notion that achieving strict euthyroidism may not be necessary for a safe surgical outcome [ – ]. However, these studies primarily assessed clinical and surgical outcomes, rather than evaluating perioperative endocrine physiology. In contrast, our prospective analysis provides novel evidence by demonstrating dynamic intraoperative and early postoperative changes in FT3, FT4, and cortisol. The consistent decline in FT3, absence of intraoperative hormone surges, and preserved cortisol recovery collectively indicate that modern anaesthetic and surgical techniques effectively mitigate physiological stress even in patients with significant biochemical hyperthyroidism. Thus, our results complement and biologically reinforce the safety outcomes reported in recent large observational studies. To our knowledge, only two studies have focused on thyroid hormone changes in the early period before and after total thyroidectomy for Graves’ disease [ , ]. One study focused solely on hyperthyroid patients [ ], while the other evaluated only euthyroid patients [ ], with neither evaluating intraoperative stress. Our study uniquely assessed both thyroid hormone and cortisol levels, alongside anaesthetic use, haemodynamic parameters, and postoperative outcomes in patients with varying preoperative thyroid function. Cortisol, a critical stress hormone, was evaluated due to its potential role in precipitating adrenal insufficiency, a condition that may exacerbate or trigger thyroid storm [ ]. Recent advances in anaesthetic management, particularly TIVA, allow for better control of analgesia and sedation, thereby minimising intraoperative stress responses [ , ]. Intraoperative cortisol levels decreased significantly in both groups, suggesting that surgical stress was effectively reduced, particularly in the hyperthyroid group. Similar results were obtained in patients with tumours who underwent total thyroidectomy during the same period (data not shown). Lower intraoperative cortisol levels in the HT group may indicate greater stress suppression by TIVA. Additionally, there were no significant differences between the groups in terms of intraoperative physiological parameters, including body temperature, blood pressure and heart rate, nor in the required doses of anaesthetic agents. These findings further support the notion that contemporary anaesthetic techniques effectively mitigate perioperative stress, even in patients who remain biochemically hyperthyroid. Serum cortisol levels increased in

stress was effectively reduced, particularly in the hyperthyroid group. Similar results were obtained in patients with tumours who underwent total thyroidectomy during the same period (data not shown). Lower intraoperative cortisol levels in the HT group may indicate greater stress suppression by TIVA. Additionally, there were no significant differences between the groups in terms of intraoperative physiological parameters, including body temperature, blood pressure and heart rate, nor in the required doses of anaesthetic agents. These findings further support the notion that contemporary anaesthetic techniques effectively mitigate perioperative stress, even in patients who remain biochemically hyperthyroid. Serum cortisol levels increased in both groups one day after surgery, with levels in the HT group tending to be higher than those in the ET group. These results suggest that cortisol secretion is not impaired in patients with hyperthyroidism or suspected subclinical adrenal insufficiency. The administration of preoperative glucocorticoids in four HT patients may have contributed to their perioperative stability. Glucocorticoids reduce the peripheral conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine and decrease thyroxine production in patients with Graves’ disease [28]. Thyrotoxicosis is associated with adrenal insufficiency [29,30], and the co-administration of steroids alleviates the risk of exacerbating this condition. Hermann et al. [ ]. reported that total thyroidectomy increased serum thyroglobulin levels but did not stimulate the release of free triiodothyronine and free thyroxine in 23 patients with severe hyperthyroidism who were pretreated with propranolol alone. Senese et al. [ ] conducted a similar study among 17 euthyroid patients with Graves’ disease, reporting increased thyroglobulin levels and decreased free triiodothyronine levels, as well as a slight increase in free thyroxine levels. Despite the previous study including only euthyroid patients, our results align with those of Senese et al. [ ]. In our study, free thyroxine levels did not change significantly overall after thyroidectomy, but a mild significant elevation was reported in the ET subgroup. The decrease in free triiodothyronine levels after thyroidectomy does not necessarily indicate that free triiodothyronine was not released from the thyroid gland into the blood during intraoperative manipulation. This is because free thyroxine was significantly elevated in euthyroid patients post-thyroidectomy, to at least some extent. The short half-life of free triiodothyronine, once released from the thyroid gland, may have counteracted this increase. Higher preoperative thyroid hormone levels, especially free triiodothyronine, are more likely to decrease postoperatively (Fig. ), which reduces the potential risk of thyroid storm. As free triiodothyronine is the primary source of systemic thyroid hormone action, a slight increase in free thyroxine in euthyroid patients is not clinically relevant in term of thyroid storm. Similar to the two studies mentioned above [ , ], the present results showed differences in thyroglobulin and thyroid hormone release during surgery, which can be attributed to thyroid hormone synthesis. Although antithyroid drugs inhibit this process, they do not affect the thyroglobulin pool, which exists in relatively large amounts in the follicular lumen in the form of colloids. Follicular cells store less thyroid hormone, and thyroid follicular colloids may be more susceptible to intraoperative manipulation than follicular cells. Surgery for Graves’ disease presents a number of technical challenges. Using advanced haemostatic devices and IONM can significantly improve surgical safety [ , , ]. Together with TIVA, these technologies may help to reduce surgical stress and complications. While IONM enhances operative precision and nerve protection, the direct influence of IONM on physiological stress responses was beyond the scope of this study. Although radioactive iodine therapy is an established alternative, many of our patients were referred from other institutions for surgery. These patients presented with conditions such as large goiters or orbitopathy, or had contraindications to medical therapy, making surgery the most appropriate option. We also addressed the timing of levothyroxine replacement therapy. According to the guidelines of the American College of Endocrine Surgeons, ATDs should be discontinued after surgery and levothyroxine therapy should typically be initiated one week after surgery in patients with hyperthyroidism at the time of surgery, in order to allow thyroid hormone levels to return to normal [ ]. At our institution, we initiate levothyroxine replacement therapy the day after surgery, except in cases of extreme hyperthyroidism. Given the rapid decline in hormone levels observed (Fig. ), early replacement therapy may help to prevent transient hypothyroidism. It is possible that high preoperative hormone levels lead to receptor desensitisation, reducing the risk of immediate postoperative hyperthyroid effects [ ]. In other words, hypothyroidism is possible during certain postoperative periods even if thyroid hormone levels are within the normal range. Mild hyperthyroidism may be preferable to hypothyroidism in terms of postoperative wound healing and overall health, but this remains to be investigated. This study has several limitations. In other words, hypothyroidism is possible during certain postoperative periods even if thyroid hormone levels are within the normal range. Mild hyperthyroidism may be preferable to hypothyroidism in terms of postoperative wound healing and overall health, but this remains to be investigated. This study has several limitations. First, it was conducted at a single high-volume endocrine surgery center, so the findings may reflect careful patient selection and institution-specific perioperative expertise. This may limit the generalizability of the findings to other settings. Second, the sample size was relatively small, and the study was not powered to detect differences in rare but clinically important outcomes, such as thyroid storm or severe postoperative complications. Third, while TIVA-enabled anaesthetic management resulted in comparable intraoperative physiological parameters between the euthyroid and hyperthyroid groups, the study was not designed to determine the specific preoperative physiological or biochemical thresholds required for safe surgery. Additionally, while IONM was routinely used, we did not directly evaluate the extent to which IONM itself contributed to reducing surgical stress. Fourth, cortisol levels were not adjusted for diurnal variation; however, all samples were collected at standardised perioperative time points, and consistent patterns were observed across groups. Finally, while the observed perioperative endocrine patterns provide physiological insight, they should not be interpreted as definitive evidence of overall surgical safety. Conclusions This study provides prospective physiological data suggesting that, in a high-volume center using contemporary perioperative management, total thyroidectomy in selected patients with Graves’ disease who are not fully biochemically controlled was not associated with exaggerated perioperative endocrine or stress responses. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as they do not establish overall surgical safety. However, they support the feasibility of surgery in carefully managed patients when euthyroidism cannot be fully achieved. Larger multicenter studies are needed to confirm these observations. documents.title: ATA Guidelines for Diagnosis and Management of Thyroid Disease During Pregnancy

chunks.content: Introduction Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a prevalent complication during pregnancy (11% in Europe doi: 10.3389/fendo.2021.691033.) and known to be associated with higher rates of preeclampsia, macrosomia, and other complications ( ). Similarly, thyroid disorders during pregnancy, including (subclinical) hypothyroidism (SCH) and thyroid autoimmunity (TAI), are common and linked to various adverse pregnancy outcomes, of which some are the same as documented in case of GDM ( ). Thyroid disorders have been associated with a higher risk of GDM via different pathways, due to increased insulin resistance (IR) in case of thyroid dysfunction, and via common inflammatory pathways in case of the presence of TAI ( , ). The initial treatment of GDM consists in dietary (Di) and lifestyle (LS) measures (DiLS), and when glycaemic targets as proposed by the international societies are not rapidly reached, insulin therapy (IT) is started ( ). Several factors have been associated with the need for IT in GDM, including advanced maternal age, body mass index (BMI) (obesity) and a history of GDM or familial diabetes ( ). Data on the impact of thyroid dysfunction on the IT need in women with GDM are limited to three studies ( , , ). One in association with women who had hypothyroidism ( ) and two others in case of hypothyroxinaemia ( , ). We had two main aims in this study. The first was to compare all baseline data (demographic, obstetric and thyroid) and thyroid disorders between women with GDM in the DiLS group versus the IT group, and the second to determine in logistic regression analyses which independent variables (demographic, obstetric and thyroid parameters/disorders and treatment) were associated with IT need in women with GDM as dependent outcome. Subjects and methods Study population and aims This cohort study results from a collaboration between the departments of Endocrinology and Gynaecology and Obstetrics in CHU Saint Pierre, a public university hospital in Brussels, Belgium. The study was approved by the institutional review board ‘Comité Local d’Éthique Hospitalier, No d’agréation: O.M. 007 AK/15-11-114/4568’. The need for written consent from study participants was waived due to the retrospective analysis of routinely collected data. In our centre, a systematic screening for GMD with an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) is done (when normal first trimester glycaemia). This is done since in our centre, many women have a high risk profile (obese, older age, and other background than Caucasian), with a reported prevalence of GDM of 19.6% ( ). Eligibility criteria comprised all women with ongoing pregnancies who performed their laboratory screening (including the OGTT) and full obstetric follow-up in our centre from the beginning of January 2013 to the end of December 2014. We included only women who performed an OGTT. As shown in , women with pre-existing diabetes, pregnant after IVF/ICSI or multiple pregnancies were excluded; finally, 328 women with GDM were stratified into two groups: group-1 ( n = 274) ‘DiLS’ treated only with diet and lifestyle measures, and group-2 ( n = 54) ‘IT’, who needed on top of the DiLS also IT to achieve correct glycaemic targets. The first aim of the study was to investigate if demographic data, obstetric history, thyroid disorders/treatment and parameters (TSH, FT4 and TPOAb) were different between both study groups. The second aim of the study was to determine variables (demographic, obstetric and thyroid) that were associated with the main study outcome, namely IT in women with GDM. For the logistic regression analyses, from the 328 women with GDM, 57 patients were excluded (seven with suppressed serum TSH, three with isolated FT4 levels and 46 who were screened for thyroid disorders >20 weeks of gestation); the regression analyses were performed on the data of the remaining 272 women. Associations with the depended outcome (IT need in women with GDM) were made with thyroxine treatment (for SCH) initiated before or after screening, thyroid parameters (TSH and FT4 levels), and thyroid disorders (SCH or TAI). For TAI, we applied a first trimester determined cut-off for TPO (≥60 kIU/L) ( ). Corrections were made for a history of GDM, parity, maternal age and BMI, tobacco use in pregnancy and foetal gender. Methods Definitions During the first antenatal consultation, demographic parameters and obstetric data were collated and routine blood tests, including serum TSH, FT4, thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAbs) and fasting glucose. An OGTT was performed at 24–28 weeks of pregnancy. Gestational age was based on ultrasound findings and expressed in full weeks and days of amenorrhoea. Smoking was stratified as yes/no (women who stopped smoking during pregnancy were also considered as smokers). GDM was diagnosed by a 75 g OGTT performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy according to the WHO criteria: fasting glucose ≥92 mg/dL or 1 h postprandial glucose ≥180 mg/dL or 2 h ≥153 mg/dL) ( ). TAI was defined

Gestational age was based on ultrasound findings and expressed in full weeks and days of amenorrhoea. Smoking was stratified as yes/no (women who stopped smoking during pregnancy were also considered as smokers). GDM was diagnosed by a 75 g OGTT performed between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy according to the WHO criteria: fasting glucose ≥92 mg/dL or 1 h postprandial glucose ≥180 mg/dL or 2 h ≥153 mg/dL) ( ). TAI was defined as TPOAb levels ≥60 kIU/L, and SCH when TSH levels were ≥3.74 mIU/L. A dietary consultation and lifestyle instructions were provided. We proposed glycaemic tests four times a day; in the morning on an empty stomach and 2 h after each meal. One week to 10 days later, blood glucose profiles were assessed. Long-acting insulin was started in the evening if fasting blood glucose remains ≥95 mg/dL in 20–30% of results, and rapid insulin was started if it remains >20–30% of postprandial blood glucose levels or were ≥120 mg/dL at 2 h ( ). Serum assays All blood test analyses were performed by the laboratory of CHU Saint Pierre. Serum TSH, FT4 and TPOAb levels were measured using the Chemiluminescence Centaur XP Siemens immunoanalyzer. Nonpregnant reference values were 0.3–4.0 mIU/L, 10.3–25.7 pmol/L and <60 kIU/L for TSH, FT4 and TPOAb, respectively. Total imprecision CVs were 6.9, 4.2 and 7.6% for TSH, FT4 and TPOAb, respectively. In a Danish study, it was determined that in pregnant women (median pregnancy week 10 (range, 4–20)), for the same assay, the 95th cut-off for TPOAb was 60 kIU/mL ( ). In a previous study, we determined institutional-specific first-trimester reference ranges for serum TSH and FT4, according to the ATA-GL recommendations ( ). The reference range for serum TSH (2.5–97.5th percentile) was 0.06–3.74 mIU/L, and 10.29–18.02 pmol/L for serum FT4. Plasma glucose was measured by an automated colourimetric-enzymatic method on a Hitachi/Roche-Modular P analyser; CV was 1%. Statistical analysis Data were stored in a Microsoft Excel database and statistical analyses performed using StatPlus:mac, Analyst Soft Inc. – statistical analysis program for macOS; version v8 ( https://www.analystsoft.com/en/ ). Descriptive statistics are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) for normally distributed and median (interquartile range (IQR)) for skewed variables. Comparison between groups was performed by Chi 2 or Fisher’s exact tests (according to the number of events) for categorical data and by Student’s T -test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous data (according to the distribution). In the section on the aims, we explained how the logistic regression analysis was performed. P values were considered significant whenever P < 0.005. Results shows baseline demographic and obstetric parameters in all women with GDM and according to the treatment type. The median (IQR) age for all women was 32 (28–36) years, and comparable between both study groups ( P = 0.856). The median BMI was 27 (23–30) kg/m 2 for all women and higher in GDM-IT vs GDM-DiLS women (28 (25–33) vs 26 (23–30) kg/m 2 ; P = 0.007). Similarly, a higher prevalence of obesity (BMI ≥ 30 kg/m 2 ) was noted (40.7 vs 24.8%; P = 0.017). Women in the GDM-IT group had a lower prevalence of high parity rate (≥2) vs those in the GDM-DiLS group (25.9 vs 39.8%; P = 0.020). No difference was noted between groups concerning the prevalence of other than the Caucasian background, smoking during pregnancy, history of miscarriage or fetal gender. shows thyroid parameters in all women with GDM and according to the treatment. Gestational age at blood sampling was 13 (11–16) weeks, and comparable between both study groups ( P = 0.242). The only parameter that tended to be different between both groups was serum FT4 (12.9 (11.6–14.2) in the GDM-IT vs 14.2 (12.9–15.1) in the GDM-DiLS group; P = 0.066). All other thyroid parameters and the prevalence of disorders were comparable between both study groups. shows the results of the multivariable logistic regression analyses. Only FT4 levels were associated with IT need in women with GDM; aOR: 0.76; 95% CI: 0.61–0.94; P = 0.011. Correction for TAI (considering a cut-off ≥60 kIU/L) did not modify the association. Other results not shown in the tables: If the cohort of patients who were included to perform the regression analyses ( n = 272) was divided into three tertiles according to their BMI’s, the prevalence of IT women in T3 (BMI: 30–51 kg/m 2 ; n = 73) was 14 vs 27% in T1 (BMI: 17–25 kg/m 2 ; n = 107); P = 0.026. The prevalence between the other tertiles was comparable (data not shown). The FT4 values were comparable between T3 and T1 (12.9 (11.9–15.4) vs 14.2 (12.9–14.2) pmol/L); P = 0.741. When the logistic regression analyses were done for each tertile of BMI separately, only for tertile-2 (the normal BMI group), an association was obtained between FT4 levels and the dependent outcome IT (aOR: 0.53; 95% CI: 0.31–0.90; P = 0.018). For the other tertiles, no significant results were observed (data not shown). Discussion The major study result was the association between lower FT4 levels and the higher prevalence of women who needed IT on top of dietary and lifestyle measurements to control their GDM, according to the international standards ( ). In several studies, low FT4 levels have been associated with a higher prevalence of GDM, but IT treatment as outcome was not considered ( , , , , , ). In addition, beyond the scope of GDM, in a longitudinal study on the progression from prediabetes to diabetes type 2, it was shown that the risk was higher with low-normal thyroid function (HR = 0.91; 95% CI: 0.86–0.97 for FT4) ( ), and in another study, subjects with the highest FT4 quartiles showed significantly lower fasting insulin and HbA1c levels ( ). On the other hand, in some studies, no association between low FT4 levels and a higher risk of GDM or IR was noted ( , ). This discrepancy can be explained by a different study setting, other assays for FT4, other gestational ages at which FT4 was measured, heterogeneity in the definition of GDM, and others. Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the association between low(er) FT4 levels and a higher prevalence of GDM. In the study by Zhang et al. , it was noted that triglyceride levels mediated 21.3% of the association between FT4 and GDM; high triglycerides are known to affects insulin sensitivity ( ). Thyroid hormone (TH) receptors are present in pancreatic β-cells and TH can stimulate β-cell proliferation and insulin secretion, important to maintain normal glucose homoeostasis during pregnancy ( ). In peripheral tissues, T3 increases glucose transporter type 4 (GLUT4) expression and mitochondrial oxidative capacity, thereby facilitating glucose uptake and utilization. A reduction in circulating FT4 may lead to insufficient T3, contribute to β-cell dysfunction and peripheral IR ( , ). TH influences glucose metabolism and may contribute to the development of GDM. With increased TH availability, glucose uptake in skeletal muscle is enhanced, endogenous glucose production rises, and insulin half-life is reduced. Both in vitro and clinical studies demonstrate that either low or high TH availability can increase IR. An alternative explanation is that isolated hypothyroxinaemia/lower FT4 levels may reflect a non-thyroidal illness process, linking it to GDM through inflammatory or metabolic pathways. It was observed that low FT4 was associated with higher fasting insulin levels, but not with fasting glucose, suggesting that increased IR in participants with low FT4 was compensated for by elevated insulin secretion. However, lower FT4 was associated with higher post-load glucose concentrations during the OGTT, indicating that compensatory mechanisms were insufficient to fully counteract the IR. Interestingly, the association between FT4 and non-fasting glucose during the OGTT varied by maternal BMI, with attenuation at higher BMI, suggesting that the influence of TH on IR may be less important compared to f.i. obesity ( , , ). This is nicely shown when we divided the cohort into three tertiles according to the BMI. The impact of FT4 on IT need was only present in the tertile with normal BMI levels. In addition, in the meta-analysis, the odds of BMI in relation to IT need was much stronger compared to that of FT4 levels (data not shown). The placenta plays an important role in the relationship between FT4 and GDM via two mechanisms. On the one hand, and excessive type 3 deiodinase, which inactivates T4 and T3, and low(er) maternal FT4 may impair placental development and function, resulting in altered nutrient transport, increased inflammation, and oxidative stress – mechanisms implicated in GDM pathogenesis ( ). On the other hand, in case of an impaired placental function, lower hCG levels will stimulate less the thyroid gland, and therefore, FT4 levels will be lower and the prevalence of GDM higher ( , ). Previous studies have shown that euthyroid women with TAI had an

role in the relationship between FT4 and GDM via two mechanisms. On the one hand, and excessive type 3 deiodinase, which inactivates T4 and T3, and low(er) maternal FT4 may impair placental development and function, resulting in altered nutrient transport, increased inflammation, and oxidative stress – mechanisms implicated in GDM pathogenesis ( ). On the other hand, in case of an impaired placental function, lower hCG levels will stimulate less the thyroid gland, and therefore, FT4 levels will be lower and the prevalence of GDM higher ( , ). Previous studies have shown that euthyroid women with TAI had an increased risk of GDM ( , ). The underlying hypotheses are that common variants in immune genes might be involved and/or that the cytokines involved in TAI (IL-6 and TNF-α) might lead to a higher degree of IR ( , , ). However, in our study, women in the GDM-DiLS group tended to have a higher prevalence of TAI compared with women in the GDM-IT group. This might be an argument in favour of the impact of TH/low(er) FT4 levels as the more important underlying mechanism, compared with that of a common inflammatory pathway. Furthermore, some studies did not observe higher rates of GDM in women with TAI ( ). Limitations of our study were that the retrospective design though the data were prospectively collected, the absence of hCG levels, TgAb status, and FT3 levels. Concerning hCG, it is known that it stimulated thyroid function and that higher levels are associated with less GDM ( ). TgAb positivity, which can occur isolated in about 5% of women without TPOAb positivity has also been associated with an impaired impact of hCG on thyroid function during pregnancy ( , ). However, TgAb positivity has not been associated with lower FT4 levels ( ). Some studies associated a higher FT3-to-FT4 ratio or only FT3 levels during pregnancy with GDM, and no association with FT4 levels ( ). However, the measurement of FT3 levels during pregnancy remains debated ( ). Conclusion Women with lower FT4 levels, a lower parity rate and a history of GDM had an increased risk for IT need on top of dietary and lifestyle measures to control their glycaemia according to the international accepted standards. These study results should be confirmed, with the measurement of interleukins, serum hCG, FT3 levels, TgAb and other placental factors, to have a better idea of the underlying mechanisms.
